abstract: mRNA has emerged as an important new class of medicines, offering new opportunities as vaccines and therapeutics. mRNA molecules are large, highly polar and fold into complex, higher-order structures, resulting in heterogeneity. Multimerisation (aggregation) is a critical quality attribute of mRNA and may affect translational efficiency or lipid nanoparticle formulation. However, mRNA multimerisation remains poorly studied, as robust analytical methods are required for characterisation and structurally distinct populations are difficult to isolate for downstream analysis. We have developed and utilised preparative-scale, non-denaturing ion-pair reversed-phase HPLC to purify distinct mRNA monomer, dimer and multimer populations. Downstream desalting using tangential flow filtration ensured no significant perturbation of purified mRNA populations. Further characterisation of the mRNA higher-order structures was performed using Atomic Force Microscopy and subsequent automated structural analysis. mRNA dimers/multimers formed structured higher-order assemblies rather than end-to-end elongations, with mRNAs maintaining a distinct shape, even during multimerisation. Purifying distinct mRNA monomer, dimer and multimer populations establishes a platform for detailed structural, biochemical and biophysical analysis of higher-order mRNA structures. These methodologies provide insight into complex mRNA secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Integrating these approaches with design strategies to enhance mRNA stability and protein expression will accelerate the development of next-generation mRNA therapeutics
